Of the eight terminals storing jet fuel, five supply commercial and general aviation. Energy Transfer’s East Boston terminal supplies the highest volume, as it serves BOS, which consumed 579 million gallons in 2024. BTV and nearby Vermont airports are supplied by Albany-area terminals. Three terminals are currently storing jet fuel solely for military use (Table 21). There are two Air Force bases in Massachusetts; one naval station in both Rhode Island and Maine; and eight National Guard bases, with at least one in each New England state (U.S. Department of Defense 2025). Military aircraft use multiple types of jet fuel including JP-8, JP-5, and Jet A. Table 22 provides airport tank farm information. Airports reported that their storage capacity represented between 3 and 5 days of fuel use. Generally, airports own the tank farm and lease it to an airline fuel consortium or fixed-based operator who manages it. Smaller airports may operate under a different scheme in which the airport either operates the fuel system or hires a third party to do so. Most large airports deliver fuel to aircraft via a fuel hydrant system (underground pipes to each gate), whereas smaller commercial airports and general aviation airports refuel aircraft by truck.
